title: Chapter 5 — Of The Use Which The Americans Make Of Public Associations In Civil Life
paragraphs: I do not intend to speak of those political associations by which men try to defend themselves against the despotic influence of a majority or against the aggressions of royal power. I have already treated that subject. Each citizen becomes more feeble as an individual, and so less able to preserve his freedom single-handed. If he did not learn, as this happens, to combine with his fellow citizens to defend it, it is clear that tyranny would inevitably grow together with equality.

Here I speak only of those associations that are formed in civil life without reference to political objects. The political associations that exist in the United States are only a single feature amid the immense number of associations in that country. Americans of all ages, all conditions, and all dispositions constantly form associations. They have not only commercial and manufacturing companies, in which all take part, but associations of a thousand other kinds: religious, moral, serious, trivial, large or small, enormous or tiny. The Americans form associations to give entertainments, to found educational institutions, to build inns, to construct churches, to spread books, and to send missionaries to the antipodes. In this way they found hospitals, prisons, and schools. If the aim is to promote some truth or to encourage some feeling by the support of a great example, they form a society. Wherever you see the government in France, or a man of rank in England, at the head of some new undertaking, in the United States you will be sure to find an association. I met with several kinds of associations in America of which, I confess, I had no previous idea. I have often admired the extreme skill with which the inhabitants of the United States manage to set a common goal before the efforts of a great many men and to get them to pursue it voluntarily. I have since traveled through England, from which the Americans took some of their laws and many of their customs, and it seemed to me that the principle of association was by no means used so constantly or so skillfully there. The English often accomplish great things alone, whereas the Americans form associations for the smallest undertakings. It is clear that the English consider association a powerful means of action, but the Americans seem to regard it as the only means they have of acting.

Thus the most democratic country on earth is the one where, in our time, men have carried to the highest perfection the art of pursuing in common the object of their common desires, and have applied this new science to the greatest number of purposes. Is this the result of chance? Or is there in reality a necessary connection between the principle of association and the principle of equality? Aristocratic communities always contain, among a multitude of people who are powerless by themselves, a small number of powerful and wealthy citizens, each of whom can carry out great undertakings single-handed. In aristocratic societies men do not need to combine in order to act, because they are strongly held together. Every wealthy and powerful citizen is the head of a permanent and compulsory association, made up of all those who depend on him or whom he makes serve his designs. Among democratic nations, on the contrary, all citizens are independent and feeble. They can do hardly anything by themselves, and none of them can oblige his fellow men to lend him their help. They all therefore fall into a state of incapacity if they do not learn to help each other voluntarily. If men living in democratic countries had no right and no inclination to associate for political purposes, their independence would be in great danger. But they might long preserve their wealth and their cultivation; whereas if they never acquired the habit of forming associations in ordinary life, civilization itself would be endangered. A people in which individuals lost the power to achieve great things single-handed, without gaining the means of producing them by united effort, would soon fall back into barbarism.

Unfortunately, the same social condition that makes associations so necessary to democratic nations also makes them harder to form among those nations than among any others. When several members of an aristocracy agree to combine, they easily succeed. Each of them brings great strength to the partnership, so the number of its members may be very small. And when the members of an association are few, they can easily get to know one another, understand one another, and set fixed rules. The same opportunities do not arise among democratic nations, where the members of an association must always be very numerous for it to have any power.

I am aware that many of my countrymen are not in the least troubled by this difficulty. They argue that the more feeble and incapable the citizens become, the more capable and active the government should be made, so that society at large may do what individuals can no longer do. They believe this answers the whole difficulty, but I think they are mistaken. A government might take the place of some of the largest American companies, and several States of the Union have already attempted it. But what political power could ever carry on the vast multitude of smaller undertakings that American citizens carry out every day with the help of the principle of association? It is easy to foresee that the time is drawing near when man will be less and less able to produce, by himself alone, the commonest necessities of life. The task of the governing power will therefore keep increasing, and its very efforts will extend it every day. The more it takes the place of associations, the more individuals will lose the idea of combining and will need its assistance. These are causes and effects that endlessly produce each other. Will the administration of the country eventually take over the management of all the manufacturing concerns that no single citizen is able to run? And if a time finally comes when, because landed property has been divided up so extremely, the soil is split into an infinite number of parcels and can be cultivated only by companies of farmers, will the head of the government have to leave the helm of state to follow the plow? The morals and the intelligence of a democratic people would be as much endangered as its business and manufactures if the government ever wholly took the place of private companies.

Feelings and opinions are renewed, the heart is enlarged, and the human mind is developed by no other means than the reciprocal influence of men upon each other. I have shown that these influences are almost nonexistent in democratic countries. They must therefore be created artificially, and this can be done only by associations.

When the members of an aristocratic community adopt a new opinion or conceive a new feeling, they give it a place, as it were, beside themselves on the lofty platform where they stand. Opinions or feelings so conspicuous to the eyes of the multitude are easily introduced into the minds or hearts of everyone around. In democratic countries the governing power alone is naturally in a position to act in this way. But it is easy to see that its action is always inadequate and often dangerous. A government is no more able to keep opinions and feelings alive and in circulation among a great people than to manage all the speculations of productive industry. As soon as a government tries to go beyond its political sphere and enter on this new path, it exercises, even unintentionally, an intolerable tyranny. A government can only dictate strict rules, the opinions it favors are rigidly enforced, and it is never easy to tell its advice from its commands. The case will be worse still if the government really believes it has an interest in preventing all circulation of ideas. It will then stand motionless, weighed down by the heaviness of voluntary torpor. Governments therefore should not be the only active powers. In democratic nations, associations ought to take the place of those powerful private individuals whom the equality of conditions has swept away.

As soon as several inhabitants of the United States have taken up an opinion or a feeling that they wish to promote in the world, they look for mutual assistance. As soon as they have found each other, they combine. From that moment they are no longer isolated men but a power seen from afar, whose actions serve as an example and whose words are listened to. The first time I heard in the United States that 100,000 men had publicly bound themselves to abstain from spirituous liquors, it seemed to me more like a joke than a serious commitment. I did not at first see why these temperate citizens could not content themselves with drinking water by their own firesides. At last I understood that 300,000 Americans, alarmed by the spread of drunkenness around them, had made up their minds to support temperance. They acted just like a man of high rank who dresses very plainly in order to inspire the humbler classes with a contempt for luxury. It is probable that if these 100,000 men had lived in France, each of them would have petitioned the government individually to keep watch over the public houses all over the kingdom.

Nothing, in my opinion, deserves our attention more than the intellectual and moral associations of America. The political and industrial associations of that country strike us forcibly. But the others escape our notice, or if we do discover them, we understand them imperfectly, because we have hardly ever seen anything like them. It must be acknowledged, however, that they are as necessary to the American people as the former, and perhaps more so. In democratic countries the science of association is the mother of science. The progress of all the rest depends on the progress it has made. Among the laws that govern human societies, there is one that seems more precise and clear than all the others. If men are to remain civilized, or to become so, the art of associating together must grow and improve in the same proportion as the equality of conditions increases.
